public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Kotzig's Conjecture

*Reference:* A. Kotzig, cited in A. Rosa, *On certain valuations of the vertices of a graph*,
Theory of Graphs (Internat. Sympos., Rome, 1966), Gordon and Breach, 1967, pp. 349–355.

Kotzig conjectured that for every $n$, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into copies of
any $n$-edge tree via cyclic shifts of a single embedding. This is strictly stronger than
Ringel's conjecture; see `Paper/RingelConjecture.lean`. The large-$n$ case is proved by
Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov; see `Arxiv/2001.02665/RingelConjecture.lean`.
-/

@[expose] public section
namespace KotzigConjecture

open SimpleGraph

/--
For any tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into
$2n+1$ edge-disjoint copies of $T$ via cyclic shifts of a single embedding.

The $2n+1$ copies are $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{2n}$ where $f_i(v) = f_0(v) + i$ for all vertices
$v$ — each copy is obtained by adding $i \pmod{2n+1}$ to every vertex of the base copy.
This is strictly stronger than `RingelConjecture.ringel_conjecture`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem kotzig_conjecture {V : Type} [Finite V]
    (T : SimpleGraph V) (hT : T.IsTree)
    (n : ℕ) (hn : T.edgeSet.ncard = n) :
    ∃ f : Fin (2 * n + 1) → (V ↪ Fin (2 * n + 1)),
      (∀ i v, f i v = f 0 v + i) ∧
      Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (T.map (f i)).edgeSet (T.map (f j)).edgeSet) ∧
      ⨆ i, T.map (f i) = (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * n + 1))) := by
  sorry

end KotzigConjecture

reformulations.difference: The MPS paper formulates Kotzig's conjecture both as a rainbow embedding in the near-distance colouring of K_{2n+1} and as a cyclic decomposition. Lean uses the latter formulation rather than explicitly mentioning edge colours.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under translation modulo q = 2n+1, each near-distance colour class is one orbit of q unordered edges. The oddness of q makes the translation action on edges free. A rainbow n-edge embedding selects exactly one edge from each of the n colour classes, so its q translates partition the complete graph. Conversely, two distinct base edges of the same colour would be nonzero translates of each other, contradicting pairwise edge-disjointness. Lean's Fin addition is modular addition, and mapping a graph along an injective vertex map gives precisely its image edges.

sources_consulted: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, A proof of Ringel's Conjecture, arXiv:2001.02665v2: https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02665 and https://arxiv.org/e-print/2001.02665 — introduction, main theorem, near-distance-colouring theorem, concluding remarks and Rosa reference.

review.notes: No mathematical defect found in the single theorem. Finite V ensures edgeSet.ncard is genuine finite cardinality; IsTree entails nonemptiness and n+1 vertices. The n=0 conclusion was proved independently in Lean. Tests passed for stars with 0–3 edges and a suitable four-vertex path placement; an unsuitable path placement correctly failed. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, sorry-free proofs establish that the file's conclusion is equivalent to one base embedding whose translates cover each edge exactly once. The source proves only the sufficiently-large-n case, consistent with retaining the all-n conjecture as research open. The original Rosa (1967) article could not be retrieved directly; the mathematical claim and attribution were verified through the explicitly cited MPS paper's introduction, which states both equivalent versions. The reviewed file was not modified.
